newsitem.title: CHINA: China's parliament debates anti-corruption law.
newsitem.headline: China's parliament debates anti-corruption law.

text.p: China's top law-making body on Tuesday opened a week-long session that was expected to pass a law to combat corruption and review systems for the election of deputies from Hong Kong to the National People's Congress.

According to an agenda passed on the first day of the session, the standing committee of the National People's Congress, or parliament, was to pass an anti-corruption law as well as the Hong Kong garrison law, the Xinhua news agency said.

Beijing has repeatedly launched crackdowns on graft, which senior leaders have called a cancer that threatens the Communist Party's grip on power. But many Chinese say enforcement of anti-corruption measures at senior levels is patchy at best.
Top prosecutors had vowed to crack down on corruption among the ranks of leading officials in the government and ruling party, state media said on Tuesday.

The Hong Kong garrison law was necessary to ensure that People's Liberation Army troops stationed in Hong Kong after China resumes sovereignty in mid-1997 would fulfil their duty according to the law, Xinhua quoted parliament law committee vice-chairman Wang Shuwen as telling the session.
Under the law, the garrison's aircraft and naval vessels, vehicles and military personnel would be exempt from checks, search and detention by Hong Kong law enforcers, Wang said.

In terms of the relationship between the garrison and the government of Hong Kong, the government would "give support" to the troops, Wang said, apparently implying that it would not have jurisdiction over the soldiers.
A draft resolution on election of deputies from Hong Kong to the parliament was also under study, Xinhua said.
The standing committee session also was to review draft amendments to the Criminal Law and a draft law on National Defence to be submitted to the annual session of parliament next March, Xinhua said.
